newsitem.title: USA: US economist Bergsten sees dlr jawboning effective.
newsitem.headline: US economist Bergsten sees dlr jawboning effective.

text.p: Currency players, for now, had clearly heeded Japan's verbal warnings about the dollar's strength, said Institute for International Economics director Fred Bergsten.
But U.S. and Japanese economic authorities should stand guard to intervene should the dollar begin to climb again, he said.

"At the moment I'm not sure there's a need for intervention," said Bergsten in an interview. "But if it looked like the dollar was about to shoot up again, it would be highly desirable for them to come in with intervention to prevent that."

The dollar has crumbled about 10 yen from just below 127 last week to below 117 in Wednesday trading after repeated calls from Japanese authorities for a halt to the dollar's sharp rally earlier this year.
"It's fascinating...that Japanese jawboning without any apparent intervention had such an impact," Bergsten said.
Bergsten has repeatedly argued that the dollar should trade closer to 100 yen, citing the yawning trade surplus that Japan enjoys with the United States.

U.S. officials led by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin have clearly tempered their previously staunch support for the dollar as they have begun to echo Japanese concerns about the weak yen, said Bergsten.
"The implication is that Treasury accepts or even welcomes the decline of the dollar that's occurred," said Bergsten.

But Bergsten, a former Carter Administration official seen by some as an influential outside adviser to the Clinton White House, stopped short of defining a current Treasury target for the dollar/yen.
"I don't know that they have a specific number," he said.
Asked about whether he thought the Federal Reserve would raise rates at its meeting next Tuesday, Bergsten said: "I think the Fed will probably not raise interest rates again.

"The softening of the American economy, the clearly good numbers on inflation, continued price stability, really obviate any requirement for another move," he said in a separate interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Bergsten added that the Fed should not be influenced by recent exchange rate movements.
"I don't think the fed will be motivated by these exchange rate movements at all, nor should it be. As I say, exchange rates are moving back in the proper direction."
